story.setting: The film takes place on November 3, 2026, beginning at 8:15 a.m. Beijing time at the Dongfeng Commercial Aerospace Innovation Testing Area, then moving to an illustrative view above Earth. The Dongfeng launch site is a flat desert launch complex beneath a pale morning sky. Lijian-2 Y2 is the ascending launch vehicle, shown with clustered booster cores, a bright exhaust plume, and a widening ground cloud. Its mission-specific appearance should follow the November 3 Xinhua photograph credited to Wang Jiangbo, not imagery from its March debut. The orbital schematic is a curved blue Earth beneath eighteen small satellite markers, presented as an explanatory graphic rather than observed footage. No people or animals appear. The vertical 9:16 film uses restrained news-documentary color: cool sky, warm exhaust, and deep orbital blue. All generated imagery is illustrative, not purported live footage.

clips.paragraph: A vertical wide shot establishes the Dongfeng launch site. Lijian-2 Y2 rises from the pad, its bright exhaust plume pushing a widening ground cloud across the desert. The camera tilts upward smoothly, keeping the clustered booster cores visible as the vehicle climbs into the pale morning sky. The narrator says, “On November third, Lijian-2 launched from Dongfeng at eight fifteen Beijing time, making its second flight.” End with the ascending vehicle centered high above the pad.

clips.reference_why: A simple animated orbital schematic can communicate the confirmed outcome without a designed reference image.
clips.paragraph: Cut to the orbital schematic: a curved blue Earth beneath eighteen small satellite markers. The camera holds a wide view as the markers illuminate together along a single illustrative orbital arc, confirming the payload count without pretending to show the actual separation sequence or final spacing. The narrator says, “Eighteen satellites from Qianfan Polar Group Twenty-One reached their intended orbit. Xinhua reported success for the rocket’s first large-scale satellite-internet deployment.” End on the complete illuminated arc.

research.caution: “Latest big launch” is not an official category; the sources confirm successful satellite deployment, not that the satellites are already operational.
research.subject: CAS Space’s Lijian-2 Y2 launch carrying 18 Qianfan constellation satellites on November 3, 2026.

looks.look: CAS Space documents a common-booster-core configuration, a total length of 53 meters, core diameter of 3.35 meters, and first-flight payload-fairing diameter of 4.2 meters. These dimensions describe the documented first-flight configuration. ([cas-space.com](https://www.cas-space.com/article/512.html?utm_source=openai))

looks.thing: November 3 launch at Dongfeng Commercial Aerospace Innovation Testing Area
looks.look: Xinhua publishes a photograph of the actual Lijian-2 Y2 liftoff, credited to photographer Wang Jiangbo; this is a mission-specific visual reference rather than footage from the rocket’s earlier debut. ([news.cn](https://www.news.cn/tech/20261103/2aeea17092b14c4a883140ba4858cbec/c.html?utm_source=openai))

facts.fact: Lijian-2 Y2 lifted off at 8:15 a.m. Beijing time from the Dongfeng Commercial Aerospace Innovation Testing Area. ([chinanews.com](https://www.chinanews.com/gn/2026/11-03/10725111.shtml?utm_source=openai))
The payload comprised 18 satellites belonging to Qianfan Polar Group 21. ([finance.people.com.cn](https://finance.people.com.cn/n1/2026/1103/c1004-40826754.html?utm_source=openai))

The satellites reached their intended orbit, and Xinhua reported the flight-test mission as successful. ([news.cn](https://www.news.cn/tech/20261103/2aeea17092b14c4a883140ba4858cbec/c.html?utm_source=openai))
This was the second flight of the Lijian-2 rocket. ([chinanews.com](https://www.chinanews.com/gn/2026/11-03/10725111.shtml?utm_source=openai))
It was Lijian-2’s first large-scale satellite-internet constellation deployment mission. ([finance.people.com.cn](https://finance.people.com.cn/n1/2026/1103/c1004-40826754.html?utm_source=openai))

The mission used a multi-satellite separation system that unlocked the stacked satellites together before their separation, rather than unlocking each satellite independently. ([chinanews.com](https://www.chinanews.com/gn/2026/11-03/10725208.shtml?utm_source=openai))

Lijian-2’s debut launched successfully at 7 p.m., carrying the Qingzhou prototype cargo spacecraft and two other satellites into their intended orbit. ([cas-space.com](https://www.cas-space.com/article/512.html?utm_source=openai))

clips.reference_why: This illustrative launch scene requires no supplied picture or designed still.
clips.prompt: 8-second silent illustrative news-documentary opening clip of Lijian-2 Y2 launching from Dongfeng Commercial Aerospace Innovation Testing Area on November 3, 2026, at 8:15 a.m. Beijing time, in vertical 9:16. Use image-to-video with the supplied November 3 Xinhua photograph credited to Wang Jiangbo as the required vehicle-appearance reference, not March-debut imagery. Photorealistic illustration, pale morning light, restrained documentary mood, fine desert texture; ascent energy is powerful and steady, never frantic. One continuous shot, with the same reference-matched clustered booster cores, launch complex, lighting and small illustrative label throughout. 0–4 s: vertical wide framing shows Lijian-2 Y2, anchored by its clustered booster cores, rising above the pad; flat desert stretches beneath a pale sky, bright exhaust feeds a widening ground cloud, and low launch structures remain small along the bottom of frame. Smoothly tilt upward to follow the ascent without losing the vehicle’s core configuration. A discreet, legible upper-left label reads “ILLUSTRATIVE”. 4–8 s: in a tighter vertical wide framing, Lijian-2 Y2, anchored by the same clustered cores, continues climbing; the pad and spreading dust cloud are now small near the lower edge. Continue the smooth upward tilt, centering the rocket high above the pad, then ease the camera to rest by 6 s and freeze that accepted composition for the final two seconds, with the vehicle and label clearly readable. Audio off: no narration, music or launch sound. Cool sky, warm exhaust and restrained contrast; measured pacing, no speed ramps. This is the film’s opening launch clip; the subsequent curved-Earth orbital schematic and eighteen satellite markers are not shown. Negatives: no people, animals, March-debut configuration, extra boosters, warped vehicle geometry, invented logos, live-footage claims, orbital views, subtitles or additional text.

clips.reference_why: A simple animated orbital schematic can communicate the confirmed outcome without a designed reference image.
clips.prompt: An 8-second illustrative news-documentary closing clip, the second and final clip of the film, shows a curved blue Earth beneath eighteen satellite markers in vertical 9:16. Use a clean digital orbital schematic, softly lit atmospheric blue, deep orbital navy, restrained documentary color, smooth graphic textures, and quiet, measured energy; this is an explanatory graphic, not observed space footage. One continuous shot with the same curved Earth, the same eighteen markers, and the same orbital arc throughout. From 0–4 seconds, in a locked-off wide view with no camera movement, eighteen small, clearly separated satellite markers illuminate simultaneously along one thin illustrative arc above Earth's curved limb; Earth fills the lower third, and the markers are evenly legible across the middle and upper frame against a dark blue background. The markers are simple diagram symbols, not realistically scaled spacecraft, and their arrangement communicates count rather than actual orbital spacing. A small, crisp label in the upper safe area reads "ILLUSTRATIVE SCHEMATIC". From 4–8 seconds, maintain the identical wide framing and locked camera as the eighteen illuminated markers hold steady above the blue limb; retain generous dark negative space around the complete arc and keep every marker visible. Hold this fully illuminated, still, readable composition for the final two seconds, from 6–8 seconds. Audio off: no narration, music, or sound effects. Finish with cool, restrained grading and unhurried pacing; no fade before the end. Negatives: no people, animals, launch-site imagery, rocket, separation animation, moving satellites, implied actual final spacing, live-footage styling, additional markers, extra labels, flicker, camera shake, or cropped arc.
